title: Do trees share through fungi?
teaches: The two kinds of root fungi and what the evidence shows about carbon passing between trees
summary: **Most land plants live with fungi in their roots.** The partnership is called a mycorrhiza, Greek for fungus-root.
**The fungus trades soil for sugar.** Its threads gather phosphorus, nitrogen and water from far more soil than roots reach, and the plant pays in sugar and fat.
**Arbuscular fungi grow inside root cells.** They partner most plant species, make no mushrooms, and are over 400 million years old.
**Sheath fungi wrap the root tip.** They partner pines, oaks, birches and other forest trees, and many make the mushrooms of autumn woods.
**One fungus can link many trees.** Mapping showed single fungi joining dozens of Douglas-firs in a stand.
**Simard reported carbon passing from birch to fir in 1997.** More passed when the fir was shaded, and the idea of a wood wide web took off.
**Karst and colleagues found the evidence thinner than the story in 2023.** Few field studies, small amounts, wide scatter, and routes through soil not ruled out.
**The trade between plant and fungus is firmly established.** Whether trees use the links to help each other is still being tested.

blocks.text: Walk through a birch wood in autumn and the fly agarics, red with white flecks, come up under the birches and nowhere else. Under the pines on the next hill there are other mushrooms, and under the beeches others again. Some fungi seem tied to particular trees, as if they needed them.

They do. Each of those mushrooms is the fruit of a mycelium wrapped round the tree's fine roots. In the 1880s the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, asked by the Prussian government to find out how to grow truffles, found the roots of every oak, beech and pine he dug sheathed in fungus, and called the pairing a **mycorrhiza**, fungus-root.[^frank] It turned out to be the rule rather than the exception. About nine in ten land plant species form mycorrhizas, from grasses and wheat to the tallest trees.

The partnership is a trade. A hypha is a fraction of the width of the finest root, so for the same cost in material a fungus can lay down hundreds of times more length, and reach soil the roots never touch. It gathers phosphorus, which barely moves in soil and runs out near a root within days, along with nitrogen and water, and passes them to the plant. In return the plant passes sugar and fats to the fungus, a share of everything it makes by photosynthesis that has been estimated at up to a fifth.[^cost]

It is not charity on either side. In 2011 Toby Kiers and her colleagues grew a plant's roots with several arbuscular fungi at once, some generous with phosphorus and some stingy, and labelled the carbon the plant sent down. The plant sent more carbon to the fungi that gave more phosphorus, and the fungi sent more phosphorus to roots that gave more carbon. Each side rewards the partner that pays.

Root fungi come in two main kinds, which do it differently. **Arbuscular fungi** push into the root and through the walls of its cells, and inside each cell they branch into a tiny tree, the arbuscule, pressed against the cell's membrane, where the trading happens. They partner about seven in ten plant species, including most grasses, crops and tropical trees. They make no mushrooms at all; they live as threads in soil and roots and as large spores in the soil. They are among the oldest of all fungal partners: in the 407-million-year-old Rhynie chert of Scotland, some of the first land plants have arbuscules in their stems, preserved in stone.

blocks.caption: The two main kinds of root fungus, each in a root cut lengthwise and magnified. Left: the fungus sheathes the root tip and threads a net between its outer cells. Right: the fungus enters the cells and branches into tiny trees.

blocks.text: **Sheath fungi**, or ectomycorrhizal fungi, stay outside the root's cells. They wrap each root tip in a felt of hyphae and thread a net between its outer cells.[^net] They partner fewer plant species, around one in fifty, but those include most of the trees of northern and mountain forests: pines, firs, spruces, oaks, beeches, birches, and the eucalypts of Australia. The sheath fungi evolved many separate times, mostly among club fungi, and they make many of the familiar mushrooms of the woods, boletes, chanterelles, fly agarics, and the truffles of lesson 6.

A sheath fungus is not tied to one tree. Its mycelium can wrap the roots of several at once, so that two trees share the same fungus. In 2010 Kevin Beiler and his colleagues in British Columbia mapped the fungi on the roots of every Douglas-fir in a small plot, using DNA to tell one individual fungus from another. Most trees were linked to others through at least one shared fungus. The best-connected tree, one of the oldest, was linked to 47 others.

Links like these raised the question of whether anything passes from tree to tree. In 1997 Suzanne Simard, then a forest researcher in British Columbia, planted paper birch and Douglas-fir seedlings side by side in a clearcut. She enclosed each seedling in a bag and fed the birch carbon dioxide carrying one rare form of carbon and the fir another, so that the carbon each one fixed could be traced.[^label] Afterwards, more labelled carbon had gone from birch to fir than the other way. When the fir was shaded and made less sugar of its own, it received more. The journal *Nature* put the paper on its cover under the phrase **wood wide web**.

blocks.caption: A model of a birch and fir labelling experiment in eight plots. Each dot is one pair of seedlings; the bar is a rough 95% range for the average.
blocks.task: Shade the fir heavily, and dig a trench

blocks.text: The idea spread far beyond the paper. Over the next twenty years it grew, in books, films and news stories, into forests where old mother trees feed their seedlings and warn their neighbours of attack through a fungal internet. In 2023 Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema went back to the field studies to see how much of that the evidence supported.

They found much less than the story. Studies that had mapped shared fungi in the field were few, and covered only a handful of forest types. Studies that found carbon or nutrients moving between trees mostly found small amounts, scattered widely from plot to plot, as the model shows, and several found none. Few had ruled out the other routes: carbon leaking from one tree's roots into the soil and being taken up by the other, or travelling through fungi that happened to be on both trees without serving either. And there was no field study showing that what passed made a difference to the tree that got it. They also counted how often the original papers were cited for more than they had found, and the count was high.

Simard and others have answered that the critique overlooked results, and the argument goes on in the journals. What both sides accept is the core of this lesson: almost every plant trades with fungi, and in forests many trees share the same fungi. Whether trees use those shared fungi to help each other, and how much, is an open question being tested, plot by plot, with better controls.

blocks.caption: Five questions on root fungi
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What does a plant get from its root fungus?
choices: Phosphorus, nitrogen and water from soil its roots cannot reach
items.why: Hyphae are far thinner and cheaper than roots, so the fungus explores much more soil and passes nutrients to the plant, which pays in sugar and fat.

items.ask: Which kind of root fungus branches into tiny trees inside the root's cells?
items.why: Arbuscular fungi enter the cells and form arbuscules. Sheath fungi stay outside the cells, wrapping the root tip.

items.ask: Why do fly agarics come up only under birches and pines?
choices: They are sheath fungi living on those trees' roots
They feed on fallen birch bark only
Birch and pine shade suits their spores
items.why: The mushroom is the fruit of a mycelium partnered with the tree's roots, so it appears where its partner trees grow.

choices: Labelled carbon passed from birch to fir, more so when the fir was shaded
Firs poisoned birches through the soil
No carbon passed between the seedlings
items.why: She fed each species a different labelled carbon and found more moving from birch to fir than back, with more going to shaded firs.

items.ask: Which was a main point of Karst and colleagues' 2023 review?
choices: Few studies had ruled out carbon moving through the soil instead of through fungi
Root fungi do not exist in forests
items.why: They accepted that trees share fungi, but found the evidence for transfer through those links thin, small and often open to other explanations.

frank.title: Frank and the truffles
frank.text: Frank never found a way to grow truffles, but in looking for them he found that the roots of the trees they grew under were wrapped in fungus, and argued, against the view that the fungi were parasites, that tree and fungus fed each other.

cost.title: What the fungus costs
cost.text: Estimates of the plant's carbon going to its fungi range widely, from a few per cent to around a fifth, depending on the plant, the fungus and how much phosphorus is in the soil. In rich soil, plants send their fungi less.

net.title: The Hartig net
net.text: The net of hyphae between a root's outer cells is named after the German forester Theodor Hartig, who drew it in 1840 without knowing it was a fungus. It is where the sheath fungus and the root trade.

label.title: Labelled carbon
label.text: Almost all carbon is carbon-12. Simard fed one tree carbon dioxide made with carbon-13, a rare stable form, and the other with carbon-14, a radioactive form, so that each tree's carbon could be measured in the other's tissues.
